question: Asbestos is a persistent public health threat in Italy, Europe and elsewhere. The WHO estimates that asbestos-related diseases like mesothelioma and lung cancer kill more than 100 000 people every year.

Though the EU recently adopted Directive 2023/2668/EU on the protection of workers from the risks related to asbestos exposure at work, more decisive action is needed to address this carcinogenic agent’s devastating impact on human health.

In order to protect the public from the threat of asbestos, a centralised and transparent registry listing all public buildings containing asbestos must be created and made available to all citizens, while a compulsory procedure must immediately be introduced to remove asbestos from school buildings in the EU, and decontaminate them.
Given that tangible measures are needed to coordinate efforts to tackle this public health emergency, could the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
How does it plan to assist Member States in monitoring the presence of asbestos in public buildings and in taking preventive and corrective measures?

Does the Commission not consider it necessary to establish an EU registry listing all public buildings containing asbestos, to demand that removal operations be carried out as a matter of urgency – particularly in the case of schools – and to punish Member States that fail to ensure the safety of students and teaching staff?
Will the Commission create funds to finance asbestos removal operations, as well as special funds to finance research into asbestos-related diseases like mesothelioma?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.6.2024) The Commission has long recognised asbestos as a hazardous material and has been promoting the protection of people and the environment from asbestos developing and enforcing EU legislation and regulations related to asbestos management and control.

For instance, the revised Asbestos at work Directive (Directive (EU) 2023/26681) establishes requirements for the protection of workers from asbestos exposure during work activities by laying down the limit values for exposure, as well as other specific requirements, including the obligations for employers to identify and address asbestos risks in buildings2.

Considering that the magnitude of the asbestos presence – as well as screening, registration and removal strategies – differs considerably among Member States and between regions, the Commission is looking at the most appropriate way to support Member States in these areas, in line with better regulation and subsidiarity principles.

The EU provides significant funding through the Recovery and Resilience Facility, which can be used to support national measures for the removal of asbestos in the context of renovations. In addition, the cohesion policy funds can support many measures related to renovations. Cohesion policy funds are implemented under shared management between the Commission and Member States.

Member States are responsible for the selection of projects. The reduction of all forms of pollution is eligible for support from the European Regional Development Fund, under the specific conditions of the fund’s regulation3 and of the programme approved by the Commission4.
1 Directive (EU) 2023/2668 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 November 2023 amending
Directive 2009/148/EC on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?

If such information is not available, the employer shall ensure an examination by a qualified operator. 3 Regulation (EU) 2021/1058 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2021 on the European Regional Development Fund and on the Cohesion Fund, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/PDF/?
